title: Supreme Court Stays BCI Action Against NALSAR Students, Upholds Right to Protest
excerpt: CJI Surya Kant criticizes Bar Council of India for barring NALSAR law graduates from enrolling as advocates, calling the intervention 'uncalled for' and affirming students' right to peaceful protest.
body:
• The Supreme Court has stayed all punitive action by the BCI against NALSAR students and faculty after the regulator barred the 2026 graduating batch from enrolling as advocates.
  • CJI Surya Kant called the BCI intervention "uncalled for" and affirmed that students have a fundamental right to protest peacefully, even against the CJI.
  • The controversy began after around 450 NALSAR students signed a campaign opposing the invitation of CJI Surya Kant as their convocation chief guest.
  • Six National Law Universities still lack current BCI approval, raising wider concerns about the regulator's relationship with India's top law schools.

BCI Bars NALSAR Graduates Over Student Campaign

The Bar Council of India found itself at the center of a constitutional storm after its chairman, Manan Kumar Mishra, issued a circular halting the enrolment of NALSAR University of Law's 2026 graduating batch as advocates. The move came in direct response to a campaign by approximately 450 NALSAR students who opposed the university's proposal to invite Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as chief guest for their upcoming convocation.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2088206536745382295

The students' representation, submitted on July 23, cited the CJI's response to a plea over police action against protesters at the "Chalo Sansad" march at Jantar Mantar on July 20. According to the students, when a lawyer sought an urgent hearing on the matter, the CJI told counsel, "Don't waste our time, and don't waste your time." When counsel offered to show video evidence of alleged police action, the CJI reportedly responded, "We are not interested in videos; we don't have time to watch."

The representation was signed by around 70 students of the outgoing 2026 batch. Within two days, about 380 more students from the 2027 to 2031 batches extended their support.

BCI's Heavy-Handed Response

The BCI asserted that students showing disrespect toward the country's highest judicial office could not become responsible advocates. The regulator further alleged campus groupism and political instigation by certain faculty members. BCI Chairman Mishra described the student protests as being "hijacked by anti-national elements seeking to destabilize India."

The move drew widespread public backlash. The BCI eventually modified its position, withdrew the enrolment ban, and closed all proceedings against the students — but not before the matter reached the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court Intervenes

A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana heard the writ petition challenging the BCI's directives. Senior Advocate K. Parameshwar, appearing for the petitioners, argued that the regulator had no business interfering in a university's internal affairs and questioned whether any formal Council meeting had authorized the chairman's action.

"Students possess a fundamental right to protest peacefully, even where their position may be mistaken."

— CJI Surya Kant, during the hearing

CJI Surya Kant agreed that the BCI's intervention was "uncalled for," emphasizing that the dispute was a direct dialogue between himself and the students. Recalling his own student leadership activities, the Chief Justice affirmed students' fundamental right to peaceful protest. Justice Bagchi also challenged whether any formal resolution had ever been passed to authorize the circular.

The Court issued formal notice to the BCI, directing it to file a counter-affidavit within two weeks while staying any coercive action against students or faculty.

Wider Pattern of BCI Overreach

The NALSAR episode is the latest in a series of conflicts between the BCI and India's top law schools. Six National Law Universities — NLSIU Bengaluru, NLIU Bhopal, NLUO Cuttack, HNLU Raipur, TNNLU Tiruchirappalli, and GNLU Gandhinagar — still do not appear on the BCI's approved list of law colleges even after a July 31, 2026 deadline lapsed. The BCI has warned that institutions without completed renewal applications will not be allowed to admit students for the 2026-27 session.

The Supreme Court itself has previously questioned the BCI's priorities, with justices observing that the regulator's real concern should be law colleges "operating out of garages" rather than interfering in the academic affairs of established institutions.

What's Next

The BCI has been directed to file its counter-affidavit within two weeks. In a pointed gesture, CJI Surya Kant welcomed the NALSAR graduates to enrol without delay and join the Supreme Court Bar, announcing that the Court would empanel them for legal aid cases — "a befitting answer to those who had attempted to create impediments in their legal careers."

The case puts a spotlight on the balance between regulatory oversight and institutional autonomy in Indian legal education, with implications for how the BCI exercises its authority over the country's premier law schools.
